destination.tagline: The world's southernmost capital of a sovereign state.
destination.description: Wellington has been New Zealand's capital since 1865. Limited land between harbour and hills makes it denser than most New Zealand cities, and the Golden Mile from the railway station to Courtenay Place is easy to walk. Beyond the main sights, Weta Workshop runs tours of its film-effects studio in Miramar, and Cuba Street is the bohemian strip of cafés, bars and music venues.

goodToKnow.title: Pack for wind
goodToKnow.detail: Wellington is nicknamed Windy Wellington, with an average wind speed of 27 km/h, so pack a windproof layer in every season.

goodToKnow.title: Tag off the bus
goodToKnow.detail: Metlink buses and trains take Snapper or contactless cards. Tag on and off buses, or you are charged the full route fare.

goodToKnow.title: Te Papa charges visitors
goodToKnow.detail: Te Papa is free for New Zealanders and people living in New Zealand but costs NZ$35 for international visitors aged 16 and over, and some exhibitions charge extra.

destination.bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the warmest, sunniest stretch, with January the sunniest month and February the warmest, for the waterfront and the hill walks.

wellington-1.bio: New Zealand's national museum, with Māori and Pacific treasures, the national art collection, an earthquake house simulation and the world's largest colossal squid specimen.

wellington-2.bio: A 609 m historic funicular from Lambton Quay up to Kelburn, first built in 1902, with a Cable Car Museum at the top.
wellington-2.hours: Mon–Thu 7:30 AM – 8:00 PM; Fri 7:30 AM – 9:00 PM; Sat 8:30 AM – 9:00 PM; Sun and public holidays 8:30 AM – 7:00 PM

wellington-3.bio: A 225-hectare forest valley inside an 8.6 km predator-proof fence, where kākā, little spotted kiwi, tuatara and takahē have been released.

wellington-5.bio: A 25-hectare hillside garden established in 1868, best known for the Lady Norwood Rose Garden, which has more than 300 varieties and is at its best from November to March.

wellington-6.bio: A special-effects studio in Miramar behind Oscar-winning work on The Lord of the Rings, open to visitors on guided tours.

wellington-8.bio: The seat of government, where the Beehive and Parliament House stand together, with free guided tours.

wellington-9.bio: A 1.2 km harbourside walk of 30 minutes to 2 hours from Kumutoto Stream, lined with sculptures such as Solace in the Wind and the 23 quotes of the Wellington Writers Walk.

wellington-10.bio: New Zealand's oldest public zoo, opened in 1906, with giraffes, meerkats, lemurs, big cats and a wildlife hospital you can watch into.

wellington-11.bio: A city wrapped around Porirua Harbour, with headland walks at Whitireia Park and Aotea Lagoon beside the water.

wellington-12.bio: The only public botanic garden in New Zealand devoted solely to native plants, with about 11 km of tracks, a canopy walkway and 7 hectares of original forest protected by Job Wilton.

wellington-13.bio: A 24.8-hectare predator-free DOC reserve and former quarantine station in Wellington Harbour, reached by East by West ferry from Queens Wharf or Days Bay, with a walking track around the island and little blue penguins.

wellington-14.bio: Wellington's city beach, rebuilt with 22,000 tonnes of sand from Golden Bay in the early 2000s, with Norfolk pines and cafés along Oriental Parade.

wellington-16.bio: A museum in the 1892 Bond Store on the waterfront, with a Wellington timeline, maritime history and the Wahine Theatre's film of the 1968 Wahine disaster; free for New Zealand residents, with a charge for international visitors.

wellington-17.bio: A sheltered beach and park walled in on three sides by bush-clad slopes, reached by ferry from Queens Wharf, and the setting Katherine Mansfield drew on for At the Bay.

wellington-18.bio: A coastal walk from the Te Kopahou Reserve visitor centre at Owhiro Bay to the red rock formation in a small scientific reserve on Wellington's south coast.

wellington-19.bio: The Thorndon house at 25 Tinakori Road where the writer Katherine Mansfield was born on 14 October 1888, a Category 1 Historic Place returned to its original layout, with a garden.

wellington-20.bio: A west-coast seaside village about 20 minutes' drive from Karori, with fishing, diving and a 7 km DOC walkway along the beach and over farmland to historic gun emplacements.

wellington-21.bio: A contemporary art gallery that opened in 1980 as the Wellington City Art Gallery and has shown exhibitions at its Victoria Street venue while its Civic Square building is closed for earthquake strengthening.

wellington-22.bio: A memorial park built in 2015 for the First World War centenary around the National War Memorial, with the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, bronze sculptures and eight international memorials.

wellington-23.bio: A digital full-dome planetarium with telescope viewing (weather permitting) and galleries on space, Matariki and Māori star navigation.
wellington-23.hours: Varies by day; evening sessions most days

wellington-24.bio: A scientific reserve whose five earthquake-raised beaches record about 7,000 years of uplift, with up to 500 fur seals hauled out each winter, reached on foot in about 45 minutes from the car park.

wellington-25.bio: A regional park of farmland and bush between Lower Hutt and Porirua, with the 1903–04 concrete Korokoro Dam, WWII ammunition stores and Belmont Trig, which looks over Porirua Harbour and the Hutt Valley.

wellington-26.bio: An art museum in Lower Hutt that opened in 1971 as the Dowse Art Gallery and was renamed in 1982, in a building remodelled in 2013.

wellington-27.bio: New Zealand's first permanent lighthouse (1859), where Mary Bennett served as the country's only female lighthouse keeper, reached on foot or by bike along an 8 km gravel coast track from Eastbourne.

wellington-28.bio: A Hutt City museum in the former wharf shed on The Esplanade in Petone, beside the wharf.

wellington-29.bio: A Porirua gallery and museum focused on Māori and Pacific art, in a 1998 building that also holds the library, a café and a Japanese garden.

wellington-30.bio: A volunteer-built mountain bike park with over 50 km of single track through 250 hectares of regenerating native bush, from family trails to technical descents.

The Te Araroa clause is cut because no loaded source supports it. Decide whether to keep it, re-bio it around Whitireia Park and Titahi Bay, or remove it.

Pukeahu (wellington-22): OWNER REVIEW. It is a memorial park, marginal against the 'minor memorial' rule. The bio says 'eight international memorials' (eight memorials, not eight countries). The Memorial Building and Carillon may be closed for seismic work, and 'Open 24 hours' is unverified. ticketUrl not added because mch.govt.nz is behind a challenge.

City Gallery (wellington-21): OWNER REVIEW, venue unclear. The Civic Square building is reported closed and citygallery.org.nz lists 67 Victoria Street. Coordinates are unchanged and probably point at the closed building, so confirm the pin. `free` was not set: WellingtonNZ says entry is free but the gallery site shows 'Book tickets'. The bio will need updating when the Civic Square building reopens.
